name: Uma Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 58, and I've been wiring and repairing places for twenty-seven years, with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm an experienced middle-level worker, about average rather than the person everyone calls for the strangest fault. I like a neat repair in a cramped shop, but lugging the case up three floors gets tiring. I use AI every day to organise my own learning notes and compare ordinary stock descriptions, always checking the actual label and job requirements.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life around the job look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Dev packs orders at a book supplier, our grown children are twenty-nine and thirty-three, and we rent a small upstairs flat. My pay is low for a licensed electrician, the reserve would cover eighteen days, and there are few other electrical firms nearby. A quiet repair week can reduce the paid hours, so the rent still feels exposed even when nothing dramatic happens. Retirement is in sight as a question, not an income or date we've managed to confirm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the others a tool can earn its place without turning every year into a new age. I'd keep the daily notes that help me and still read the actual fitting. Hype hasn't been paying our rent in either direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lose paid hours in a quiet week, and eighteen days saved is not much padding. Dev's packing wage helps, but our present total leaves little room after rent. The plateau would remove one uncertainty, not make our existing low pay comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop buying workday lunches and coffees, aiming for 45 a month left for bills after any extra food costs at home, rather than promise a new savings deposit. I'd carry lunch in the old food box and keep current licensed repair work and checked daily AI notes through the next year. I'd look at the actual bills with Dev each month, without putting a pension or either grown child's money into the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about another short paid week, with a small thing I can change today. The food box won't solve the pay rate. I'd still feel better opening the account knowing which cost we'd actually stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How firm is the 45 figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean a spending target, not money already earned or a guaranteed saving. If prices or an unpaid day swallowed the difference, I'd write the real figure down. A lunch box can reduce a bill without becoming a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell somebody who called you the technology expert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the licensed work stays mine to do and check, whether or not a screen gave me the wording. I'm not a master electrician or running the business. An ordinary wage and a finished safe repair are enough to want a fair week.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without treating hype as either a wage or an excuse to ignore the actual fitting.
I'd separate **ordinary repair work** from stories about a new technological age.
think: My **paid hours** could fall in a quiet week, with only eighteen days of expenses in reserve.
Dev's wage helps, but **low combined slack** leaves the rent exposed despite little AI change.
do: Stop **bought lunches and coffees** now, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home.
Keep **current licensed repairs** and checked daily AI notes, reviewing real bills with Dev monthly.
feel: **Anxious about short weeks**, able to stop a small real cost without pretending the pay problem has disappeared.
S0.quote: A lunch box can reduce a bill without becoming a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Her **baseline insecurity** comes from low pay, variable paid hours and eighteen days saved, rather than invented losses on the plateau.
The **45 target** concerns reduced spending for bills, not guaranteed income, investment or a chosen additional saving deposit.

steps.text: Stop bought lunches and coffees; target 45 monthly for bills net of extra home food costs
Keep current licensed repairs and checked daily notes; review actual bills monthly with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm planning and ordering can change before anybody sends a robot up the stairs. I'd volunteer to try turning my spoken completed-job notes into an AI draft, because typing them after a long call-out is dull. I'd still want the actual paid week counted rather than just the minutes the office saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if quicker ordering and notes meant more repairs fitted into fewer paid days. Dev's physical packing should be less directly exposed, though the supplier's screen work changes first. With our small reserve, a modest cut in my wage would be a household problem, not a clever efficiency story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the employer for two practice sessions on the new AI voice-note draft, only with permission, free inside paid shifts and normal weekly wages and hours maintained. I'd check every draft against the completed job before real use and keep doing current licensed repairs through the first year. I'd also stop bought workday lunches and coffees, targeting the same 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home, not counting on a new qualification or deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the paid hours, but keen to try a specific nuisance I can actually measure. I don't have to dislike a new method to worry about the wage attached to it. I'd want both questions on the table at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the draft with my own completed-job record before it went anywhere. If it invented a reading or a part, I'd stop that draft and correct the record rather than send a smoother falsehood. I've used AI daily without giving it the right to decide what happened in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the trial had been worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count whether it made the note clearer inside paid time, not whether I could finish unpaid at home. If the firm wouldn't maintain wages and hours, I wouldn't take the practice sessions. A quicker note is useful only if the electrician still gets a paid week.

say: I'd distinguish **planning and ordering** from later physical automation, offering a concrete trial rather than a general promise.
I'd count **the paid week** alongside time saved on completed-job notes.
think: My **paid days** could shrink when administration gets faster, making even a modest cut significant with eighteen days saved.
Dev's **physical packing** looks less directly exposed than the supplier's screen work, without making our household secure.
do: Practise **two AI voice-note sessions** only with employer permission, free in paid shifts, maintaining normal weekly wages and hours.
Keep **licensed repairs**, checking drafts against completed jobs before use and stopping invented readings or parts.
Stop **bought lunches and coffees** now, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home.
feel: **Anxious but keen**, wanting a useful method while treating possible lost wages as a separate real concern.
S1.quote: A quicker note is useful only if the electrician still gets a paid week.
fieldNote: Her **new voice-note practice** extends daily AI use, conditional on employer permission, free paid time and unchanged weekly wages and hours.
Her **draft checks** remain tied to completed work; ordinary licensing does not become master status or authority delegated to software.

steps.text: Practise two employer-approved AI voice-note sessions free during paid shifts, maintaining normal weekly wages and hours
Keep licensed repairs; compare drafts with completed-job records before use; stop invented readings or parts
Stop bought lunches and coffees; target 45 monthly for bills net of extra home food costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends thinking work changes in 2028, while capable physical robots follow around 2031. I'd be 60 first and 63 later, which leaves real working years to account for rather than a neat retirement escape. I'd start asking local repair firms about paid vacancies now, not wait for a machine to come through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a substantial loss of my paid repair hours by the robot stage, with pressure on planning and office time earlier. Eighteen days saved wouldn't carry that loss far, and Dev's packing hours could also face capable robots. I'd be awake trying to make the rent add up, even while I could still take practical steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd contact the few local firms for licensed repair vacancies while keeping my present job and stopping bought workday lunches and coffees, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home. I'd leave only after a signed offer confirmed weekly take-home pay at least equal to my current normal week and travel within twenty minutes each way without extra cost. In 2029 I'd take only actually offered paid work within my licence and ability, reviewing real household resources with Dev rather than assume a pension or future vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large loss of household hours, not too frightened to make the calls. I'd rather hear a disappointing vacancy answer now than build the rent around a job that never existed. There isn't much room to confuse a possibility with a paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the hours and pay in writing, then work out the take-home amount and the actual journey. A higher hourly figure can still mean fewer paid hours in the week. I can't pay the rent with an impressive rate on an empty timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the local firms had nothing suitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the present paid work while it was actually offered and bring the real figures back to our household discussion. The grown children wouldn't become an income line without an actual offer of help, and I wouldn't assume Dev could cover any shortfall. We would need confirmed resources before agreeing that either of us could stop.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from physical robots around 2031, keeping my ages of 60 and 63 distinct.
I'd contact **local repair firms now**, rather than assume retirement or a vacancy would arrive at the right time.
think: I expect **substantial repair-hour loss** by the robot stage, with earlier administrative pressure and little cash to bridge it.
Dev's **packing hours** could also face capable robots, leaving the rent exposed to more than one lost wage.
do: Seek **local vacancies now**; require signed pay at least current normal weekly take-home, journeys within twenty minutes each way without extra cost.
Stop **bought lunches and coffees** now, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home.
Keep **2029 offered paid work** within licence and ability, reviewing actual resources with Dev without assuming pensions or future vacancies.
feel: **Alarmed but acting**, losing sleep over substantial household hours while making calls and distinguishing vacancies from signed offers.
S2.quote: I can't pay the rent with an impressive rate on an empty timetable.
fieldNote: Her **search is actual**, but a move remains conditional on signed weekly earnings and affordable travel; no replacement job is guaranteed.
The **2029 work plan** depends on real offers and ability, while any later exit needs confirmed household resources rather than age alone.

steps.text: Contact local repair firms now; keep the present job until a suitable signed offer
Require at least current normal weekly take-home; travel maximum twenty minutes each way without extra cost
Stop bought lunches and coffees; target 45 monthly for bills net of extra home food costs
Keep actually offered paid work in 2029 within licence and ability; review resources with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2031 gives us five years to ask better questions, with capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and then 66, not automatically drawing an affordable retirement income. I'd still make the local vacancy calls now instead of making older people sound like one settled group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big cut in my ordinary repair hours by the robot date, though the earlier office changes could already affect paid time. More preparation matters, but our current thin reserve and low pay still make a short week worrying today. I can't say the future gap will be funded simply because it is further down the page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd contact local firms now for licensed repair vacancies, keeping my job until a signed offer provided at least my current normal weekly take-home pay and a journey within twenty minutes each way without extra cost. I'd stop bought lunches and coffees, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home rather than forecasting a pot of savings five years ahead. I'd keep current licensed repairs and in 2032 review actual resources, ability and offered work with Dev before any affordable stopping decision we both agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the large hours cut I expect later, with more thinking space than the fast card. I still feel today's short reserve when the rent date comes round. A longer warning helps the search; it doesn't put a second local firm in an empty building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would experience make a new offer likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask any employer for the actual paid schedule and full weekly figure, not just praise for experience. I'm licensed and reasonably experienced, not a specialist they must hire. I can ask clearly without inventing the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the 2032 review need to establish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the income amounts and start dates we could actually confirm, with our real costs and whether work was physically manageable. If stopping wasn't affordable, we'd need to see that honestly rather than choose a date to make the form tidy. I wouldn't promise a job at 64 or money from a grown child.

I'd avoid **assumed retirement income**, because being 63 or 66 doesn't establish what the household can afford.

fieldNote: Her **later resource review** checks real income dates, costs, ability and offers, without manufacturing pension entitlement or continued work capacity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets a household check more than one version of the budget, with thinking AGI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd be 68 and then 71, which makes pretending to know my working body especially silly. I'd still want a fairer actual wage now, not ten years of being told to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical repair work looks less directly threatened by AI over the next few years, but our paid hours can already dip and the eighteen-day reserve is still thin. The distant dates don't make today's rent safe. I don't know what resources or capacity we'd have at 69, so I wouldn't use a future job as the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the local vacancy enquiries now under the same signed-offer rule: at least my current normal weekly take-home pay and journeys within twenty minutes each way without extra cost before leaving. I'd keep current licensed repairs and stop bought lunches and coffees, targeting 45 monthly for bills after extra food costs at home. In 2037 I'd review actual resources, costs, ability and real offered work with Dev, with any exit needing confirmed affordability and our agreement rather than a guessed pension or job at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present household margin, even with less near-term physical AI pressure. I could be interested in the wider changes and still check the rent account before buying lunch. Being curious is not the same as having money put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide whether you kept working later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check at the time whether I could do a real offered task safely under my licence, not announce a ten-year physical promise today. Dev's position and our actual costs would matter too. A budget can ask for work that a body or an employer cannot supply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you include the grown children in that budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the family the actual figures if we wanted help discussing them, not assign either grown child a wage contribution. They have lives and bills of their own. I'd rather find the missing amount on paper before anybody mistook a possible family conversation for an income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a big loss of physical paid hours after the earlier thinking changes, with little reserve for either stage. Written weekly pay, an affordable journey and actual income figures would help more than a promise that older workers would somehow be fine. I don't need a future that admires my licence while leaving my paid week blank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how long a cheap lunch plan can carry a low wage. It can help with a bill, but I don't want that little choice mistaken for a solution to the rate or the lack of nearby firms. I'd like the chance to keep doing ordinary competent work for a week that covers our life.

headlineQuote: I don't need a future that admires my licence while leaving my paid week blank.
portrait: Uma, **58**, is an experienced middle-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician’s licence, doing ordinary repairs at about average skill.
Her **low pay**, eighteen-day reserve and few local firms expose rent shared with book-packer partner Dev; their children are grown.
She uses **AI daily**, choosing protected new voice-note practice only in Steady Disruption and keeping responsibility for actual job checks.
Her **AGI job search** requires signed weekly earnings and affordable travel; later decisions depend on actual resources and ability.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected substantial repair-hour losses after earlier thinking changes, with little household reserve for either stage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written weekly pay**, affordable travel and actual income figures would support a real household decision instead of an assumed older-worker escape.
